His son, the newly-proclaimed King Haakon VIII, has inherited the Norwegian throne. item.title: Austria museum heist: Thieves snatch diamond necklace
item.description:
Albert Otti/picture alliance via Getty Images Thieves have stolen a 200-carat platinum-and-diamond necklace worth several million dollars during a brazen heist at Vienna’s Museum of Applied Arts. The Van Cleef and Arpels necklace, designed for the former royal family of Egypt and worn by Queen Nazli in 1939 at her daughter’s wedding, was set with 673 precious stones. It was one of 500 pieces included in an exhibit devoted to the French jewelry designers that had been on display since June. On Thursday, two men bought tickets to enter the museum, smashed the necklace’s glass display case with a hammer, and then ran in an unknown direction, police said. The thieves did not wear masks and were clearly seen on surveillance cameras. The exhibit, scheduled to run until September 27, was closed immediately after the theft. item.title: Iceland votes on whether to resume EU membership negotiations
item.description:
Icelanders will decide tomorrow whether to resume talks on joining the EU in a vote that has taken on deeper significance in the wake of US President Donald Trump’s threats in the Arctic. Polls in the tiny island nation — which does not have armed forces — are almost evenly split. Supporters believe joining the European bloc could give the country greater protection and boost its economy, while critics worry over sovereignty. The Arctic has emerged as a key battleground between global superpowers: Trump has threatened to take over Greenland, an autonomous territory belonging to Denmark. Meanwhile, China is flexing “ its economic muscle in partnership with Russia ” as melting ice caps open up new navigable routes around the Arctic, Bruegel wrote. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

item.title: Bernie Sanders, AOC join marchers in Washington to ‘defend the vote’
item.description:
Sixty-three years after the March on Washington, thousands gathered Friday in the nation's capitol for a Defend the Vote rally and warned that voting rights are under attack again. Earlier this year, the Supreme Court weakened a key provision of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, making it harder for people to challenge voting maps they argued were racially discriminatory. Tylik McMillan, national director of youth and college for the NAACP and one of the speakers at Friday's march, joins CBS News to talk about the day.

item.description:

item.title: USS Abraham Lincoln to visit port in Thailand after more than 250 days at sea
item.description:
W hen I was deployed at sea as a junior officer , I used milestones to track the passage of time. Each day counted toward something: a port call, when you get a break on land from the monotony at sea; the “crossing the line ceremony” when a ship crosses the equator (unfortunately, canceled at the last minute for my ship); and, eventually, the date I knew that, no matter what, I would be going home. Even on my worst days, that end point helped me stay focused on the mission and gave me something to be hopeful for. The USS Abraham Lincoln left its home port of San Diego in November and was scheduled to return home in May. That did not happen. In the middle of this month, it surpassed more than 240 consecutive days at sea—one of the longest deployments on record—and had only a brief working port call early last month, where it appears sailors did not disembark, leaving them still at sea…

item.description:

item.title: Tim Curry, the prolific performer who transformed for the screen – video
item.description:
As a performer, Tim Curry knew how to walk a fine line. Even his most sinister characters had an ironic sort of appeal, because watching Curry have fun is, in itself, fun. The actor, who died yesterday at age 80, acted with palpable glee: He could produce a real-life version of the Grinch’s ever-widening grin and could commit to sheer silliness in a way that freed him to twirl around in a cape while singing a gibberish song about Halloween . Perhaps nowhere was this more evident than in the 1985 film Clue . When the raucous comedy adaptation of the classic whodunit board game debuted in theaters, Paramount Pictures had a unique plan: Instead of one ending, the movie would have three, and audiences never knew which resolution—which killer, in which room, with which weapon—they were going to see.
